What is Command Line Interface (CLI)?
In the 1970s an 1980s, command line input was commonly used by Unix systems and PC systems like MS-DOS and Apple DOS.
Common CLIs include Bash (Linux/macOS), CMD and PowerShell (Windows, Zsh, Git Bash, and cloud-specific tools like Azure CLI, AWS CLI, and Google Cloud SDK).
Unlike GUI-based tools that often log user actions, CLI commands may not be logged by default, which can make tracing malicious or accidental changes more difficult.
On systems with limited memory or processing power, such as embedded devices or headless servers, CLIs are preferred because they require minimal resources.
When managing servers or cloud environments remotely, a CLI is often the only available interface.
Tasks like batch file processing, system backups, or software deployment can be automated using shell scripts in a CLI, which is more efficient than manually repeating actions in a GUI.

From flashing firmware to providing real-time access to logs, memory usage, and sensor data, CLI tools are highly beneficial in cases where technical teams must deploy software in remote or inaccessible locations.
